idiom_name: abstract record Op + one sealed record per operation + switch expression
implementation_notes: From C# 9 the algebra is a sealed record hierarchy (`abstract record Op;` plus one `sealed record Get(...)` per operation) and the interpreter is a single `switch` expression whose arms deconstruct the records with property/positional patterns: the visitor class disappears and programs stay pure, structurally comparable values. Unlike Java's sealed interfaces, the C# compiler does not prove coverage over a sealed hierarchy (CS8509 covers only enums and bool), so totality is enforced by a final `_ => throw new UnreachableException()` arm and a test that walks the algebra - the price of the idiom, not a reason to abandon it. Prefer this realization when you own the operation set and execute it in-process.
pitfalls: There is no exhaustiveness proof over a sealed record hierarchy: omitting an arm compiles and only fails in the `_` arm at run time, so keep that arm throwing and add a test that enumerates the algebra.
Record equality is structural only over the members the record declares: adding a mutable array/collection member silently changes equality and breaks value-based test expectations.
Switch expressions over nullable inputs need an explicit null arm; otherwise the null case throws NullReferenceException before any pattern runs.

variants.name: System.Linq.Expressions trees interpreted or translated by an ExpressionVisitor
variants.implementation_notes: An `Expression<Func<...>>` lambda is compiled into a data structure instead of IL, and an ExpressionVisitor interprets, rewrites or translates that tree - this is how LINQ providers turn a C# query into SQL, how mocking libraries read call specifications, and how `Expression.Lambda(...).Compile()` turns the program back into executable code. It is the library-grade realization of the same idea with the algebra fixed by the runtime (call, member, binary, lambda nodes), so prefer it when the program's meaning must travel to another runtime (database, remote service, query planner); use records plus switch when you own the algebra and interpret it locally.
variants.code_sketch:
Expression<Func<int, int>> program = x => x + 42;      // code as data
var visitor = new Rewriter();                          // ExpressionVisitor subclass
Expression rewritten = visitor.Visit(program.Body);    // interpret / transform
var run = Expression.Lambda<Func<int, int>>(rewritten, program.Parameters).Compile();
Console.WriteLine(run(1));                             // 43
pitfalls: Expression trees cannot contain statement bodies (no blocks, loops or assignments in the lambda): the algebra is fixed by the runtime, unlike records the application owns.
Compile() uses reflection emit and is expensive per call; cache the compiled delegate or interpret through a visitor in hot paths.
